analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers cancel a person's coverage after they get sick.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the health reform law's ban on insurance rescissions, never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased a rule in the 2010 health care law that stops health insurers from canceling ("rescinding") someone's policy after the person is covered — most often after that person gets sick or files a big claim. It also would have removed the requirement that insurers warn enrollees before canceling their coverage. The bill was introduced by one member in the final weeks of the session, picked up no cosponsors, and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, health insurers would gain the ability to revoke coverage retroactively once a policyholder becomes sick or submits costly claims, and to cancel coverage without giving advance notice. Insurers could keep premiums lower by shedding the sickest, most expensive customers from their rolls.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 2712 of the Public Health Service Act, added by the Affordable Care Act, which bars a health plan or issuer from rescinding coverage once an enrollee is covered, and repeals the accompanying requirement of prior notice before cancellation [S3].
The change is effective as of the date of enactment, meaning the protection would have been stripped immediately rather than phased out [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on people with individual and employer coverage who develop expensive conditions: they could lose their insurance retroactively after illness, often after having paid premiums for months or years, and would face uncovered medical bills or the difficulty of getting new coverage with a documented condition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick policyholders who lose coverage retroactively

drawbacks.text: Rescission prohibitions work both ways: a repeal restores insurers' ability to revoke coverage for fraud or intentional misrepresentation on an application, which supporters of such rules argue protects the risk pool [S3].

With the anti-rescission rule gone, patients who believed they had permanent coverage could face retroactive cancellations and large out-of-pocket bills at the moment they are sickest, and the advance-notice requirement that gave enrollees time to arrange new coverage would also be repealed [S2,S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insurers, the bill removes a constraint on revoking coverage from expensive enrollees, which could modestly reduce premiums for the healthy by shifting costs to the sick. But the human cost is direct and concentrated: people diagnosed with cancer, heart disease, or other costly conditions could lose the coverage they were paying for, precisely when they need it. On balance the bill trades a broad, severe risk for sick Americans for a benefit that is diffuse and mostly flows to insurers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and no committee action, hearing, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Ackerman (D-NY) introduced the bill on November 29, 2010, near the end of the 111th Congress [S1,S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which was the only action the bill ever received [S5,S3].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the Affordable Care Act's prohibition on rescissions remained in force [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with pre-existing conditions and anyone who becomes seriously ill: they keep the federal protection that stops insurers from retroactively canceling their coverage after they get sick. Health insurers, who would have gained the power to rescind policies, were worse off under the actual outcome.

for.name: Rep. Gary Ackerman (D-NY)
for.role: Sponsor; the bill's only supporter in Congress

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after referral; never scheduled the bill for consideration

against.name: 111th Congress
against.what_they_did: Expired on January 3, 2011 with the bill still pending in committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape was never tested [S4,S5].

industries.note: Repealing the rescission ban would return to insurers the power to retroactively cancel policies of enrollees who become expensive — after they pay premiums, before their claims are honored. Ordinary people with costly conditions would bear that cost directly, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against patients' interests [S2,S3].

The rescission ban covers group plans as well as individual coverage; repeal would allow group plans to rescind coverage once an employee is enrolled, shifting risk onto covered workers and their families [S3].
